title: 1 Kings 10:14–29
context: The chapter closes with a description of Solomon’s wealth: annual gold income, golden shields, an ivory throne overlaid with gold, gold drinking vessels, a fleet of ships of Tarshish, tribute from all the earth, chariots and horsemen, silver as common as stones, and horses and chariots imported from Egypt and exported to Hittite and Syrian kings. Solomon exceeds all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom, and all the earth seeks to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. Some figures differ slightly in the parallel in 2 Chronicles 9, such as the weight of gold in the smaller shields. Many readers notice that the final verses echo the warnings of Deuteronomy 17:16–17 against a king multiplying horses, returning to Egypt for them, and amassing silver and gold, and some see a quiet foreshadowing of Solomon’s turn in chapter 11, where the warning about wives is broken. The text itself describes rather than comments here. Both traditions read the list as narrative and description, honoring God’s gift while noticing the warning signs.

verses.text: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents of gold,
verses.arminianNotes:
The weight of gold that comes to Solomon in one year is six hundred sixty-six talents. The same figure appears in 2 Chronicles 9:13.

Arminian readers note that the amount represents enormous wealth, and that the narrative presents it as evidence of God’s blessing while setting the stage for the warnings that follow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that some readers have sought symbolic meaning in the number, but the text gives it as a figure for annual income, and readers should be cautious about reading later symbolism back into it. The amount is often estimated at roughly 20 metric tons.

Both traditions read the verse as description of Solomon’s wealth.

verses.text: in addition to that which the traders brought, and the traffic of the merchants, and of all the kings of the mixed people, and of the governors of the country.
verses.arminianNotes:
This is besides what came from traders and merchants, from all the kings of the mixed peoples, and from the governors of the land. Wealth comes from many sources.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s prosperity came through trade and tribute as well as direct gifts, and that wealth gained through legitimate commerce is not condemned in itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the sources listed show Solomon’s influence over the region, a fulfillment in part of the blessings promised to David’s line, while the accumulation of wealth will soon be set against the standard of Deuteronomy 17:17.

Both traditions read the verse as description that later narrative will place in moral context.

verses.text: King Solomon made two hundred bucklers of beaten gold; six hundred shekels of gold went to one buckler.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon makes two hundred large shields of beaten gold, each using six hundred shekels of gold. The figure matches 2 Chronicles 9:15.

Arminian readers note that the golden shields were ceremonial rather than practical, displaying royal splendor, and that their later loss to Shishak (14:26) shows how quickly such treasures can be lost.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the shields will be taken in Rehoboam’s reign and replaced with bronze (14:26–27), a sobering picture of how glory fades when a kingdom turns from the LORD.

Both traditions read the verse as description, while noting its later irony in the narrative of 1 Kings.

verses.text: He made three hundred shields of beaten gold; three minas of gold went to one shield; and the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
verses.arminianNotes:
He makes three hundred shields of beaten gold, each using three minas of gold, and puts them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 9:16 gives three hundred shekels per shield.

Arminian readers note that the difference in units between Kings and Chronicles may reflect different measuring conventions, but the exact relationship is uncertain and need not be forced.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the House of the Forest of Lebanon was a large royal hall described in 7:2–5, and that the display of golden shields there emphasized the king’s majesty. A mina is often estimated at about 600 grams.

Both traditions hedge the numbers and read the verse descriptively.

verses.text: Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with the finest gold.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king makes a great ivory throne and overlays it with the finest gold. The throne symbolizes royal authority.

Arminian readers note that the magnificence of the throne reflects the honor of the office God had given Solomon, and that such honor carries responsibility to rule with justice and righteousness (10:9).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the throne of David’s son is a recurring biblical theme, and that Christians in both traditions see in the Davidic throne a pointer to the reign of the Messiah, though the verse itself simply describes Solomon’s throne.

Both traditions read the description as narrative showing the glory of Solomon’s reign.

verses.text: There were six steps to the throne, and the top of the throne was round behind; and there were armrests on either side by the place of the seat, and two lions standing beside the armrests.
verses.arminianNotes:
The throne has six steps, a rounded back, armrests on each side, and two lions standing beside the armrests. The details are carefully described.

Arminian readers note that the lions may symbolize royal power, and possibly the tribe of Judah (compare Genesis 49:9), though the text does not explain their meaning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the precise symbolism of the throne’s features is not stated, and readers should avoid elaborate allegory; the description serves to show the unmatched splendor of Solomon’s court.

Both traditions hold the symbolism lightly and read the description as narrative.

verses.text: Twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other on the six steps. Nothing like it was made in any kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
Twelve lions stand on the six steps, one at each end, and nothing like it was made in any kingdom. The throne is unique.

Arminian readers note that the twelve lions may correspond to the twelve tribes, though this is a suggestion rather than a statement of the text, and that the throne’s uniqueness reflects the extraordinary blessing of Solomon’s reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the claim that nothing like it was made in any kingdom underscores that Solomon’s glory exceeded that of other kings, fulfilling God’s promise of riches and honor (3:13).

Both traditions read the verse as description of God-given splendor, without allegorizing it.

verses.text: All King Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. None were of silver, because it was considered of little value in the days of Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes:
All Solomon’s drinking vessels are gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon are pure gold; silver was considered of little value in his day. The abundance is extraordinary.

Arminian readers note that the narrator’s remark about silver underlines how much wealth Solomon had, while the warning in Deuteronomy 17:17 against amassing silver and gold quietly stands in the background.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God had promised Solomon riches he did not ask for (3:13), so this abundance is first a fulfillment of that promise, even as the narrative will show the danger of wealth for the king’s heart.

Both traditions read the verse as description that later events place in moral context.

verses.text: For the king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with Hiram’s fleet. Once every three years the fleet of Tarshish came bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king has a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with Hiram’s fleet, and once every three years it brings gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks. The cargo is exotic.

Arminian readers note that ships of Tarshish likely refers to a type of large seagoing vessel rather than a specific destination, and that the exact identity of some animals listed is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the word rendered peacocks is debated, with some translations reading baboons, and that the voyages show the reach of Solomon’s trade; the text does not specify the route.

Both traditions hedge the details and read the verse as description of Solomon’s far-reaching wealth.

verses.text: So King Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
So King Solomon exceeds all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. The summary statement is sweeping.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s preeminence fulfills God’s promise at Gibeon (3:12–13), and that the greatness of the gift makes Solomon’s later turning more tragic and his responsibility greater.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God gave Solomon both what he asked for, wisdom, and what he did not ask for, riches and honor, displaying God’s generous grace; the summary sets Solomon’s reign at its height before the decline of chapter 11.

Both traditions see God’s promise fulfilled and the stage set for the warning of the next chapter.

verses.text: All the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom which God had put in his heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the earth seeks Solomon’s presence to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. The source of his wisdom is named.

Arminian readers note that the nations are drawn by wisdom that God gave, and that Israel’s calling was to be a light that draws others to the LORD, a calling Solomon at this point fulfills.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator again credits God as the source of Solomon’s wisdom, so that the attention of the nations ultimately honors God, not Solomon, in keeping with the hope of Solomon’s own prayer (8:60).

Both traditions treat this verse as shared ground: God’s wisdom draws the nations to himself.

verses.text: Year after year, every man brought his tribute, vessels of silver, vessels of gold, clothing, armor, spices, horses, and mules.
verses.arminianNotes:
Year after year, everyone brings tribute: silver and gold vessels, clothing, armor, spices, horses and mules. The flow of gifts is constant.

Arminian readers note that the regular tribute shows Solomon’s influence and the peace of his reign, and that God’s blessing extended to Israel’s relations with the surrounding nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the inclusion of horses in the tribute prepares for the notices in verses 26–29, where the accumulation of horses recalls the warning of Deuteronomy 17:16; the narrative description is building toward that quiet contrast.

Both traditions read the verse as description of Solomon’s prosperity and influence.

verses.text: Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He kept them in the chariot cities and with the king at Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon gathers chariots and horsemen, fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, stationed in chariot cities and with him in Jerusalem. The military buildup is notable.

Arminian readers note that many readers hear an echo of Deuteronomy 17:16, which warned the king not to multiply horses, and that Solomon’s choices here may signal a growing reliance on military strength.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator records the facts without comment, but placed against Deuteronomy 17:16–17 they read as a quiet warning that some see foreshadowing Solomon’s turn in chapter 11; the text leaves the reader to weigh it.

Both traditions hedge the connection and read the verse as description that raises a question.

verses.text: The king made silver as common as stones in Jerusalem, and cedars as common as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king makes silver as common as stones in Jerusalem and cedar as plentiful as sycamore in the lowland. The imagery is hyperbolic.

Arminian readers note that the vivid comparison celebrates the prosperity of Solomon’s reign, while the background warning of Deuteronomy 17:17 against greatly multiplying silver and gold invites reflection.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the abundance is presented as a sign of blessing, yet the same abundance will be part of the setting in which Solomon’s heart turns away, showing how God’s gifts can become occasions of temptation.

Both traditions read the verse as description that combines celebration with an implicit caution.

verses.text: The horses which Solomon had were brought out of Egypt. The king’s merchants received them in droves, each drove at a price.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon’s horses come from Egypt, and the king’s merchants receive them in droves at a price. Some translations read Kue, a region in Cilicia, where the WEB has droves.

Arminian readers note that the import of horses from Egypt echoes the specific warning of Deuteronomy 17:16 against returning the people to Egypt to multiply horses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the reading Kue or droves is debated, and that either way the text records a significant trade in horses; many readers see a quiet signal that the king is moving away from the law’s ideals.

Both traditions hedge the translation and read the verse as narrative that the next chapter will interpret.

verses.text: A chariot was imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for one hundred fifty shekels; and so they exported them to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Syria.
verses.arminianNotes:
A chariot is imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver and a horse for a hundred fifty, and they are exported to all the kings of the Hittites and Syria. Solomon becomes a trader in arms.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s role as a middleman in the horse and chariot trade shows his commercial skill, though it also places him in the very pattern Deuteronomy 17:16 warned against.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the chapter ends with this trade notice immediately before chapter 11 opens with Solomon’s many foreign wives, so that the reader moves from abundance to apostasy; many see the sequence as intentional, though it is not stated.

Both traditions read the close of the chapter as a quiet warning held within narrative description.
